root.stem: A 14-year-old girl is brought because over the past year her voice has deepened and her muscles have grown. At birth her external genitalia looked ambiguous, with a small phallus and partly fused labia, and she has been raised as a girl. On examination she has no breast development but normal pubic hair, the phallus is now 4 cm long, a small gonad is felt in each labioscrotal fold, and a short vagina ends blindly. Pelvic ultrasound shows no uterus. Karyotype is 46,XY. Serum testosterone is in the normal adult male range, and the ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is high. Serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone and electrolytes are normal.
root.oneliner: 14F raised as a girl + ambiguous genitalia at birth + deepening voice and muscle growth at puberty + no breasts, normal pubic hair + phallus growth + gonads in labioscrotal folds + blind vagina, no uterus + 46,XY + normal male testosterone, high testosterone-to-DHT ratio + normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone
highlight: voice has deepened and her muscles have grown
no breast development but normal pubic hair
small gonad is felt in each labioscrotal fold
ratio of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) is high

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A 46,XY disorder of sex development. The clincher: **46,XY with ambiguous external genitalia at birth that virilize at puberty + normal male testosterone with a high testosterone-to-DHT ratio**.

nodes.q: Which hormone conversion fails?
nodes.note: The type 2 isoenzyme (SRD5A2 gene) is missing.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern does it follow?
nodes.note: It shows only in 46,XY individuals; it clusters in some inbred communities, for example in the Dominican Republic.

nodes.q: Which structures fail to masculinize before birth without DHT?
nodes.a: The external genitalia and the prostate
nodes.note: DHT drives the genital tubercle, urogenital folds and urogenital sinus to form the penis, scrotum and prostate.

nodes.q: Which internal duct system still develops normally because it needs testosterone alone?
nodes.a: The Wolffian (mesonephric) ducts: epididymis, vas deferens and seminal vesicles

nodes.q: Which hormone from the testes explains why she has no uterus?
nodes.a: Anti-Mullerian hormone from the Sertoli cells
nodes.note: It makes the Mullerian (paramesonephric) ducts regress, so no uterus or fallopian tubes form.

nodes.q: Why does she virilize at puberty?
nodes.a: The pubertal surge of testosterone acts directly on androgen receptors
nodes.note: The type 1 isoenzyme in skin and liver also makes some DHT. Facial hair stays sparse and the prostate stays small.

nodes.q: Which drug group blocks this same enzyme on purpose?
nodes.note: Used for benign prostatic hyperplasia and male-pattern hair loss. Pregnant women should not handle crushed tablets because they can block masculinization of a male fetus.

nodes.q: What guides management of gender and the gonads?
nodes.a: A multidisciplinary team, led by the patient's own gender identity
nodes.note: Many affected people raised as girls adopt a male gender identity at puberty; decisions on surgery and the gonads wait for the patient's input where possible.

nodes.q: A 46,XY teenager raised as a girl with no uterus could have androgen insensitivity syndrome. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both are 46,XY with testes, no uterus and a blind vagina, but puberty goes in opposite directions.

split.note: **Normal female genitalia at birth + breast development at puberty + scant pubic and axillary hair + no virilization**
**Ambiguous genitalia at birth + virilization at puberty with no breasts + normal pubic hair + high testosterone-to-DHT ratio**

nodes.q: Ambiguous genitalia with virilization could suggest congenital adrenal hyperplasia (21-hydroxylase deficiency). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **46,XX with ovaries and a uterus + high 17-hydroxyprogesterone**, often with salt wasting in infancy
**46,XY with testes and no uterus + normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone and electrolytes**

image_prompts.root: A pastel teaching illustration of hormone molecules flowing from a testis toward a lock-and-key enzyme drawn as a cracked, blocked key, beside a normally formed internal duct system of epididymis and vas deferens; no text or labels.

root.stem: A newborn boy is delivered at 36 weeks to an 18-year-old mother who smoked through the pregnancy. A maternal serum screening protein made by the fetal liver and yolk sac was high at 16 weeks. Loops of thickened, matted small bowel protrude through a 3-cm defect just to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, with no membrane covering them. He has no other visible anomalies, a normal-sized tongue and a normal blood glucose. Later in the first week, a blind-ending loop of small bowel is found at surgery.
root.oneliner: Newborn M, 36 weeks + 18-year-old mother who smoked + high maternal serum screening protein + thick, matted bowel through a 3-cm defect right of a normal cord + no covering membrane + no other anomalies + blind-ending small bowel loop at surgery
highlight: made by the fetal liver and yolk sac was high
just to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A full-thickness abdominal wall defect beside the umbilicus. The clincher: **uncovered bowel coming through a defect to the right of a normally inserted umbilical cord, with no membrane**.

nodes.q: Which developmental mechanism does its link with maternal smoking and vasoconstrictive drugs point to?
nodes.a: Vascular disruption of the developing abdominal wall (abnormal involution of the right umbilical vein or right vitelline artery)
nodes.note: This is why the defect sits to the right of the cord. Unlike omphalocele, the bowel never sits inside the umbilical cord.

nodes.q: Which maternal factor is most strongly linked to it?
nodes.note: Smoking and vasoconstrictive drugs (for example cocaine or decongestants) add risk.

nodes.q: Why is his exposed bowel thick and matted?
nodes.a: Contact with amniotic fluid inflames the bowel wall (chemical serositis)

nodes.q: Which bowel anomaly found at surgery is its classic association?
nodes.note: Chromosomal and other organ anomalies are uncommon, unlike omphalocele.

nodes.q: Which long-term bowel problem can follow atresia or loss of damaged bowel?
nodes.note: Poor bowel motility after repair also means long dependence on intravenous nutrition.

nodes.q: Which second-trimester maternal screening marker is raised?
nodes.note: Made by the fetal liver and yolk sac; it leaks from the exposed bowel. Also raised in omphalocele and open neural tube defects; ultrasound confirms the defect.

nodes.q: What is done right after birth?
nodes.a: Cover the bowel in a sterile bowel bag or plastic wrap and give intravenous fluids, with nasogastric decompression
nodes.note: The uncovered bowel loses heat and fluid fast; keep him warm.

nodes.q: Which surgery follows?
nodes.a: Primary closure, or staged reduction in a silo with delayed closure

nodes.q: Bowel outside the abdomen at birth could also be omphalocele. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both raise maternal serum AFP and both put bowel outside the abdomen, but only one has a covering sac.

split.note: **Midline defect at the umbilicus with bowel (often liver) inside a membrane sac and the cord inserting into the sac**; often with trisomy 13 or 18, heart defects or Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
**Defect to the right of a normal cord + no membrane + bowel only + rarely other anomalies**

nodes.q: A bulge at the umbilicus could be an umbilical hernia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Skin-covered bulge at the umbilicus that grows with crying and usually closes by age 4 to 5**; linked to Down syndrome and congenital hypothyroidism
**Bare, uncovered bowel outside the body from birth**

image_prompts.root: A pastel illustration of a newborn in a diaper lying under a warmer, with loops of uncovered, thickened bowel coming out through a small defect just to the right of a normal umbilical cord.

root.stem: A newborn girl has a 6-cm midline sac at the base of the umbilical cord that contains bowel and part of the liver, covered by a thin, shiny membrane, with the cord inserting into the sac. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) was high at 16 weeks. She weighs 4.6 kg, her tongue is large and protrudes, and her right leg is visibly larger than her left. Her blood glucose is 30 mg/dL at 2 hours of age. Her heart sounds are normal.
root.oneliner: Newborn F + 6-cm midline sac at the cord base with bowel and liver + thin shiny membrane, cord inserts into sac + high maternal serum AFP + 4.6 kg + large protruding tongue + one leg larger + glucose 30 at 2 hours
highlight: midline sac at the base of the umbilical cord
bowel and part of the liver
covered by a thin, shiny membrane
right leg is visibly larger than her left

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A midline abdominal wall defect at the umbilicus. The clincher: **abdominal organs in a membrane-covered sac with the umbilical cord inserting into the sac**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same defect.

nodes.q: Which normal developmental event failed?
nodes.a: Return of the physiologically herniated midgut from the umbilical cord into the abdomen (by about week 10 to 12)
nodes.note: Failure of the lateral body folds to close the midline is the other part of the explanation.

nodes.q: Which layers make up the covering sac?
nodes.a: Amnion and peritoneum (with Wharton jelly between them)
nodes.note: The sac protects the bowel from amniotic fluid, so the bowel is usually healthy, unlike gastroschisis.

nodes.q: Which syndrome do her large size, large tongue, larger leg and low blood sugar point to?
nodes.note: An imprinting defect at chromosome 11p15 that leads to overexpression of insulin-like growth factor 2 (IGF-2).

nodes.q: What causes her low blood sugar?
nodes.a: Too much insulin from enlarged pancreatic islets (hyperinsulinism)

nodes.q: Which kidney tumor is she at higher risk of?
nodes.note: Hepatoblastoma risk is raised too.

nodes.q: How is she screened for these tumors?
nodes.a: Abdominal ultrasound every 3 months until about age 7, with serum alpha-fetoprotein every 3 months until about age 4
nodes.note: The ultrasound looks for Wilms tumor; alpha-fetoprotein looks for hepatoblastoma.

nodes.q: Which test is sent for every omphalocele because of its strong link with aneuploidy?
nodes.note: Trisomy 18 and trisomy 13 are the classic associations. Echocardiography is also done because heart defects are common.

nodes.q: How is a giant omphalocele that contains liver usually treated?
nodes.a: Staged or delayed closure (for example topical treatment to let the sac skin over, then later repair)
nodes.note: Small defects with only bowel can be closed primarily. Protect the sac and keep it moist and covered at birth.

nodes.q: Bowel outside the abdomen at birth could also be gastroschisis. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both raise maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, but only omphalocele has a sac and frequent other anomalies.

split.note: **Defect to the right of a normal cord + no membrane + thick, matted bowel only**; young mother, rarely other anomalies
**Midline sac covered by a membrane + cord inserting into the sac + liver often inside**; trisomies and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome

nodes.q: A bulge at the umbilicus could be an umbilical hernia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Covered by normal skin, grows with crying and usually closes by age 4 to 5**
**Covered by a thin membrane (no skin) with the cord inserting into it + liver or bowel inside**

image_prompts.root: A pastel illustration of a large newborn in a diaper with a big tongue and a midline, shiny membrane-covered sac at the base of the umbilical cord containing bowel and part of the liver.

root.stem: A 46-year-old woman who has had three children has had heavier and more painful periods for the past year, and she now feels tired. Her pelvic examination shows a uniformly enlarged, soft, boggy and tender uterus about the size of a 12-week pregnancy, with no irregular bumps, a mobile uterus and normal adnexa. She has no pain with bowel movements and no trouble getting pregnant in the past. Her pregnancy test is negative. Her hemoglobin is 9.8 g/dL with small, pale red cells. Her periods began at age 12 and were never painful until her forties.
root.oneliner: 46F, three children + 1 year of heavier, more painful periods + fatigue + uniformly enlarged, soft, boggy, tender uterus (12-week size), no irregular bumps + mobile uterus, normal adnexa + no pain with bowel movements, no infertility + negative pregnancy test + microcytic anemia + painless periods until her 40s
highlight: uniformly enlarged, soft, boggy and tender uterus
no pain with bowel movements and no trouble getting pregnant

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Endometrial tissue growing inside the muscle wall of the uterus. The clincher: **heavy, painful periods in a woman in her 40s who has had children + a uniformly enlarged, soft, boggy, tender uterus**.

nodes.q: Where in the uterus is the misplaced endometrial tissue found?
nodes.note: Endometrial glands and stroma lie deep in the muscle, well below the endometrial-myometrial junction; the surrounding muscle thickens, so the whole uterus enlarges evenly.

nodes.q: Which part of her obstetric history raises her risk?
nodes.note: Prior uterine surgery such as cesarean delivery or curettage also raises the risk.

nodes.q: Which hormone does the trapped tissue depend on, so that it fades after menopause?
Which type of anemia explains her tiredness and small, pale red cells?
nodes.a: Iron deficiency anemia from heavy menstrual blood loss

nodes.q: In a woman aged 45 or older with heavy bleeding, which test rules out endometrial hyperplasia or cancer?
Which imaging test is used first to support the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is used when ultrasound is unclear and shows a thickened junctional zone. The definitive diagnosis is made on the hysterectomy specimen.

nodes.q: Which first-line treatment controls bleeding and pain while keeping the uterus?
nodes.note: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and combined hormonal contraceptives are other options; also treat the iron deficiency.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment once she no longer wants children?
Her enlarged uterus with heavy periods could suggest leiomyoma (fibroids). How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both enlarge the uterus and cause heavy periods in women in their 40s.

split.note: **Firm, irregular, nodular (bumpy) enlarged uterus**; well-circumscribed whorled smooth muscle tumors; often not tender
**Uniformly enlarged, soft, boggy, tender uterus** with painful periods

nodes.q: Endometrial tissue in the wrong place with painful periods could suggest endometriosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal-sized, often fixed uterus + adnexal mass (chocolate cyst), painful bowel movements, pain with intercourse and infertility**; often younger women
**Enlarged, boggy uterus + mobile uterus with normal adnexa**; endometrial tissue inside the uterine muscle

nodes.q: Her painful periods could suggest primary dysmenorrhea. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painful periods from the teenage years with a normal pelvic exam**, caused by prostaglandins
**Pain that starts in the 40s + uniformly enlarged, boggy uterus + heavy bleeding**

image_prompts.root: A pastel cross-section of a uniformly enlarged, globular uterus with small islands of endometrial tissue scattered through the thickened muscle wall.

root.stem: A 26-year-old man has had two painful sores on his penis for 5 days. They began 1 week after unprotected sex with a sex worker during a trip abroad. Each ulcer is soft, with a ragged, undermined edge and a gray-yellow, pus-covered base that bleeds when touched. A tender, swollen, fluctuant lymph node is felt in his left groin. Gram stain of the ulcer base shows gram-negative coccobacilli lined up in long parallel chains. A rapid plasma reagin test is negative, and a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test of the ulcer for herpes simplex virus is negative.
root.oneliner: 26M + unprotected sex abroad + two painful, soft penile ulcers with ragged undermined edges and a pus-covered base + tender fluctuant one-sided groin node + gram-negative coccobacilli in parallel chains + syphilis and herpes tests negative
highlight: two painful sores on his penis
soft, with a ragged, undermined edge
gram-negative coccobacilli lined up in long parallel chains
rapid plasma reagin test is negative

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A sexually transmitted genital ulcer disease. The clincher: **painful, soft ulcer with a ragged, undermined edge + tender groin node that turns fluctuant**.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A small gram-negative coccobacillus. Exam memory hook: 'It's so painful, you do cry (ducreyi)'.

nodes.q: The way the bacteria line up on Gram stain has a classic name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called 'railroad tracks': long parallel chains of coccobacilli.

nodes.q: Which growth factor does it need in culture?
nodes.note: It grows slowly on enriched chocolate-type agar; culture is insensitive, so most cases are diagnosed clinically.

nodes.q: What can the fluctuant groin node do if left alone?
nodes.a: Rupture through the skin as a suppurative bubo
nodes.note: About half of patients get a tender inguinal node; it can drain pus and leave a sinus.

nodes.q: Why does this infection raise his risk of acquiring human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection?
nodes.a: Its genital ulcers break the mucosal barrier and fill with HIV target cells
nodes.note: Ulcer-forming sexually transmitted infections (chancroid, syphilis, genital herpes) raise HIV acquisition the most. Candida, Cryptococcus and cytomegalovirus are the reverse: they follow immune damage from HIV rather than opening the door to it.

nodes.q: How is the diagnosis usually made?
nodes.a: Clinically, once tests for syphilis and herpes simplex virus are negative
nodes.note: A probable diagnosis needs painful ulcers, a typical appearance with or without tender nodes, a negative syphilis test (darkfield or serology at least 7 days after onset) and a negative herpes test. Test for HIV as well.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: A single oral dose of azithromycin 1 g (or a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone 250 mg)
nodes.note: Alternatives: ciprofloxacin for 3 days or erythromycin for 7 days. Treat sex partners from the 10 days before symptoms began.

nodes.q: How is a fluctuant node managed?
nodes.a: Needle aspiration or incision and drainage
nodes.note: Drainage relieves pain and prevents spontaneous rupture; antibiotics alone may not shrink it fast enough.

nodes.q: His genital ulcer could suggest primary syphilis. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both are genital ulcers with groin nodes after unprotected sex.

split.note: **Single painless, hard (indurated) ulcer with a clean base + painless rubbery nodes on both sides**; positive syphilis serology or darkfield spirochetes
**Painful, soft ulcer with a ragged, pus-covered base + tender, fluctuant node**; gram-negative coccobacilli in chains

nodes.q: His painful sores could suggest genital herpes. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: Both are painful; herpes ulcers start as blisters.

split.note: **Clusters of small vesicles on a red base that break into shallow ulcers**; positive herpes simplex PCR; multinucleated giant cells on Tzanck smear
**Deep, ragged, purulent ulcers with no preceding vesicles**; herpes PCR negative

nodes.q: His ulcer could suggest granuloma inguinale. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless, beefy-red ulcer that bleeds easily, with no true lymph node enlargement**; Donovan bodies in macrophages
**Painful, purulent ulcer + tender fluctuant node**

image_prompts.root: Soft pastel teaching illustration of a Gram-stained smear seen through a microscope: small pink gram-negative coccobacilli lined up in long parallel chains like a school of fish, scattered among neutrophils; clean style, no text

root.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had irregular vaginal bleeding for 3 weeks, 4 months after suction evacuation of a hydatidiform mole. She now coughs up blood-streaked sputum and is short of breath. She has lost weight, feels hot all the time, and has a fine tremor of her hands. Her uterus is slightly enlarged, and a soft bluish-purple nodule is seen on the anterior vaginal wall. Her serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin (beta-hCG) level is 240,000 mIU/mL and has risen on each of the last three checks. Ultrasonography shows both ovaries enlarged with many thin-walled cysts. A chest x-ray shows many round nodules of different sizes in both lungs. Tissue from repeat uterine curettage shows sheets of atypical trophoblast cells with hemorrhage and necrosis and no chorionic villi.
root.oneliner: 32F + 4 months after a molar pregnancy + irregular vaginal bleeding + coughs up blood + heat intolerance and tremor + bluish vaginal nodule + beta-hCG 240,000 and rising + enlarged cystic ovaries + many round lung nodules + atypical trophoblast with hemorrhage, no villi
highlight: 4 months after suction evacuation of a hydatidiform mole
has risen on each of the last three checks
both ovaries enlarged with many thin-walled cysts
many round nodules of different sizes in both lungs

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A malignant tumour of placental trophoblast that spreads early through the blood. The clincher: **rising beta-hCG after a pregnancy + bleeding + lung nodules, with trophoblast but no villi**.

nodes.q: Which two trophoblast cell types make up the tumour?
nodes.note: Both are malignant and mixed together, with large areas of hemorrhage and necrosis; the tumour has no blood vessels of its own and invades vessels instead.

nodes.q: Which type of hydatidiform mole more often progresses to this tumour?
nodes.note: Gestational trophoblastic neoplasia follows about 15 to 20% of complete moles but under 5% of partial moles. Overall, about half of choriocarcinomas follow a molar pregnancy, a quarter a miscarriage or ectopic pregnancy, and a quarter a normal pregnancy.

nodes.q: By which route does it spread?
nodes.note: Trophoblast normally invades maternal vessels, so the malignant version reaches distant organs early.

nodes.q: Which organ is the most common site of metastasis?
nodes.note: Round 'cannonball' nodules and coughing up blood.

nodes.q: After the lungs, which site is next most common, as in this patient?
nodes.note: A soft, bluish-purple nodule. Brain and liver metastases mark high-risk disease.

nodes.q: Bleeding into metastases at which site is a classic cause of death in this tumour?
nodes.note: Very vascular deposits bleed easily; sudden headache, seizures or focal deficits in a woman with rising beta-hCG suggest a bleeding brain metastasis.

nodes.q: What must you avoid doing to the vaginal nodule?
nodes.note: Metastases are very vascular and can bleed heavily. The rising beta-hCG is enough to start treatment.

nodes.q: Why does she feel hot and have a tremor?
nodes.a: Beta-hCG stimulates the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor
nodes.note: Human chorionic gonadotropin and thyroid-stimulating hormone share the same alpha subunit, and their beta subunits are similar; very high levels cause hyperthyroidism.

nodes.q: What are the cysts in her enlarged ovaries?
nodes.note: Caused by very high beta-hCG over-stimulating the ovaries; they shrink once the level falls.

nodes.q: Which test tracks how well treatment is working?
nodes.note: Measured weekly until normal, then monthly for about a year. Effective contraception is needed during follow-up so a new pregnancy does not confuse the result.

nodes.q: What is the main treatment?
nodes.note: Low-risk disease: single-agent methotrexate (or dactinomycin). High-risk disease such as hers (very high beta-hCG and many lung metastases): multi-agent chemotherapy such as EMA-CO (etoposide, methotrexate, dactinomycin, cyclophosphamide, vincristine). Cure rates are high even with metastases.

nodes.q: Which enzyme does methotrexate block?
nodes.note: Less tetrahydrofolate means less thymidine and purine synthesis, so fast-dividing trophoblast cannot make DNA.

nodes.q: A rising beta-hCG after her mole could suggest an invasive mole. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both follow a molar pregnancy and both cause persistently high beta-hCG.

split.note: **Swollen chorionic villi invading the myometrium**; usually stays in the uterus and rarely spreads far
**Sheets of malignant trophoblast with no villi + early spread through the blood to lungs and vagina**

nodes.q: Her history of a molar pregnancy could suggest a retained or recurrent mole. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Grape-like swollen villi + 'snowstorm' ultrasound + uterus large for dates**, found during a pregnancy
**Months after the pregnancy ends + no villi + distant metastases**

nodes.q: A trophoblastic tumour months after pregnancy could suggest a placental site trophoblastic tumour. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Intermediate trophoblast making human placental lactogen + only mildly raised beta-hCG**; resists chemotherapy, so hysterectomy is the treatment
**Cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast + very high beta-hCG**; very sensitive to chemotherapy

root.stem: A 38-year-old woman has had tender, lumpy breasts for 2 years. The pain affects both breasts, is worst in the week before her period, and eases once bleeding starts. Examination shows several ill-defined rubbery nodules in the upper outer quadrants of both breasts and one smooth, mobile, 2-cm mass in the left breast. There is no nipple discharge, no skin dimpling or nipple retraction, and no enlarged axillary lymph nodes. Ultrasonography shows the mass is a simple fluid-filled cyst. Needle aspiration yields clear straw-colored fluid, and the mass disappears.
root.oneliner: 38F + 2 years of tender lumpy breasts + both sides, worst before menses, eases with bleeding + rubbery nodules in both upper outer quadrants + smooth mobile 2-cm mass + no discharge, skin change or axillary nodes + simple cyst on ultrasound + clear fluid, mass gone after aspiration
highlight: worst in the week before her period
ill-defined rubbery nodules in the upper outer quadrants
no skin dimpling or nipple retraction
clear straw-colored fluid, and the mass disappears

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common benign breast condition in women aged 20 to 50. The clincher: **lumpy, tender breasts on both sides that worsen before each period**, with cysts that vanish on aspiration.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The older name; 'change' is preferred because it is not a disease in most women.

nodes.q: What drives the monthly swelling and pain?
nodes.a: Cyclic estrogen and progesterone stimulation of breast tissue
nodes.note: Symptoms track the menstrual cycle and usually settle after menopause unless she takes hormone therapy.

nodes.q: Which three features make up the classic nonproliferative histology?
nodes.note: Cysts can look bluish from outside ('blue-dome' cysts). Apocrine metaplasia means cyst-lining cells with pink granular cytoplasm.

nodes.q: Which histologic subtype carries the highest risk of later breast cancer?
nodes.note: Nonproliferative change (simple cysts, fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia): no added risk. Proliferative change without atypia (ductal hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, papilloma): about 1.5 to 2 times. Atypical hyperplasia: about 4 to 5 times.

nodes.q: Which imaging test best shows whether a palpable lump in a woman under 40 is a cyst or solid?
nodes.note: Under 30, ultrasound alone first; aged 30 to 39, ultrasound or diagnostic mammography; 40 and over, diagnostic mammography plus ultrasound.

nodes.q: After aspiration, which finding would send the fluid for cytology or the lump for biopsy?
nodes.a: Bloody fluid or a mass that remains after aspiration
nodes.note: Clear fluid with complete resolution needs only a recheck in 4 to 6 weeks; a cyst that keeps refilling also needs tissue.

nodes.q: How is her breast pain managed?
nodes.a: Reassurance, a well-fitting support bra and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)
nodes.note: Danazol or tamoxifen are reserved for rare, severe pain because of side effects.

nodes.q: Her mobile 2-cm mass could suggest a fibroadenoma. How do you tell them apart?
nodes.note: The trap: both are smooth, mobile benign lumps in young women.

split.note: **Single, firm, rubbery, very mobile mass that is solid on ultrasound and does not collapse on aspiration**; usually under 30; may grow a little with estrogen (pregnancy, before menses)
**Cyclic tenderness in both breasts + fluid-filled cyst that collapses on aspiration**

nodes.q: A breast lump at 38 could suggest breast cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hard, fixed, irregular, usually painless mass + skin dimpling, nipple retraction or axillary nodes**; solid on imaging
**Tender, cyclic, both breasts + simple cyst that disappears with clear fluid**

nodes.q: Benign breast symptoms could suggest an intraductal papilloma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody nipple discharge from one duct**, often with a tiny lump under the areola
**No nipple discharge + cyclic pain and lumps in both upper outer quadrants**

image_prompts.root: Soft pastel medical illustration of a cut section of breast tissue showing several small round blue-dome fluid-filled cysts surrounded by pale fibrous stroma, with a needle draining a clear straw-colored cyst; inset microscopy of a cyst lined by pink granular apocrine cells; clean teaching style, no text

root.stem: A 30-year-old man who has just returned from 6 months of work in Papua New Guinea has a sore on the shaft of his penis that has slowly grown over 2 months. It does not hurt. The ulcer is beefy red, with a rolled edge and a moist, granular base that bleeds easily when touched. A firm, nontender swelling lies under the skin of his right groin, but no enlarged lymph nodes are felt. A tissue smear stained with Giemsa shows dark, rod-shaped bodies with a safety-pin look inside the cytoplasm of macrophages. A rapid plasma reagin test is negative.
root.oneliner: 30M + back from Papua New Guinea + painless penile ulcer growing over 2 months + beefy red, rolled edge, bleeds easily + firm groin swelling under the skin, no enlarged nodes + Giemsa: dark safety-pin rods inside macrophages + syphilis test negative
highlight: firm, nontender swelling lies under the skin of his right groin
no enlarged lymph nodes are felt
dark, rod-shaped bodies with a safety-pin look inside the cytoplasm of macrophages
rapid plasma reagin test is negative

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A slowly destructive genital ulcer infection, mostly from the tropics (Papua New Guinea, southern Africa, India, Brazil, Caribbean). The clincher: **painless, beefy-red ulcer that bleeds easily + no true lymph node enlargement**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same infection.

nodes.q: Which organism causes it?
nodes.note: A gram-negative, encapsulated intracellular rod, formerly called Calymmatobacterium granulomatis.

nodes.q: What are the safety-pin rods inside his macrophages called?
nodes.note: Seen on Giemsa or Wright stain of a crushed tissue smear or biopsy; the bacteria stain darker at both ends.

nodes.q: The firm groin swelling is not a lymph node. What is it called?
nodes.note: A granuloma spreading under the skin of the groin; true lymph node enlargement is unusual.

nodes.q: Which cancer can arise in a long-standing, untreated lesion?
nodes.note: Chronic disease also causes genital scarring, destruction of tissue and lymphedema of the genitals.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Azithromycin for at least 3 weeks and until all lesions have healed

nodes.note: Twisting of the spermatic cord that cuts off the blood supply of the testicle; a surgical emergency. The clincher: **sudden severe testicular pain + high-riding testicle with a horizontal lie + no rise of the testicle when the inner thigh is stroked**.

nodes.note: A smaller second peak occurs in newborns, where the whole cord twists above the tunica vaginalis (extravaginal torsion).

nodes.q: Stroking his inner thigh normally makes the testicle rise. What is this reflex called?
nodes.note: Its absence on the painful side is the most sensitive bedside sign of torsion.

nodes.q: Which nerve carries the motor limb of this reflex?
nodes.a: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1 to L2)
nodes.note: The sensory limb runs in the femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve and the ilioinguinal nerve; the motor limb makes the cremaster muscle contract.

nodes.q: His other testicle also lies horizontally. Which inborn anomaly lets the testicles twist freely?

nodes.q: Which structure twists?

nodes.note: Low-pressure veins close before the artery, so the testicle swells with blood; then arterial inflow stops.

nodes.q: The testicular artery that is finally cut off arises from which vessel?
nodes.a: The abdominal aorta, just below the renal arteries
nodes.note: The left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein; the right drains straight into the inferior vena cava.

nodes.q: If this testicle later developed a tumor, to which lymph nodes would it spread first?
nodes.note: The testicle drains along the testicular vessels to nodes near the renal arteries; the scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

nodes.q: Which outcome follows if the twist is not undone within about 6 hours?
nodes.note: About 90% of testicles are saved when detorsion is done within 6 hours; salvage falls sharply after 12 to 24 hours.

nodes.q: When the diagnosis is uncertain, which test shows the cut-off blood flow?
nodes.a: Color Doppler ultrasound of the scrotum
nodes.note: Shows absent or reduced flow and sometimes a twisted cord (whirlpool sign). When the story and examination are typical, go straight to surgery without waiting for imaging.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?

nodes.note: The trap: both give a painful swollen testicle, and delaying surgery for torsion costs the testicle.

nodes.q: A twist could involve only the appendix testis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small tender nodule at the top of the testicle with a blue dot sign; cremasteric reflex present, testicle in normal position**; treated with rest and pain relief
**Whole testicle tender, high and horizontal; absent cremasteric reflex**

nodes.note: The commonest cause of acute scrotal pain in younger boys (7 to 12 years).

nodes.q: His swollen scrotum could suggest a hydrocele. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless swelling that lights up with a penlight (transillumination)**; fluid in a patent processus vaginalis or tunica vaginalis

nodes.q: Which two ligaments give the main apical support to the uterus and upper vagina?
nodes.note: The round ligament and broad ligament give little support. The cardinal ligament is also called the transverse cervical ligament.

nodes.q: Which artery runs in the cardinal ligament and is clamped at hysterectomy?
nodes.note: The ureter passes just beneath it ('water under the bridge'), so the ureter is at risk when the artery is clamped.

nodes.note: Other risks she has: older age, loss of estrogen after menopause and a chronic cough that raises abdominal pressure. Obesity, constipation and connective tissue disorders such as Ehlers-Danlos syndrome also add risk.

nodes.q: Why does menopause weaken her pelvic support?

nodes.q: If the whole uterus later comes out past the vaginal opening and stays out, which kidney problem can follow?

nodes.q: Which device placed in the vagina holds the uterus up without surgery?

nodes.q: If she declines a pessary and does not wish to keep her uterus, which operation is done?

nodes.note: A malignant gland tumor of the prostate in an older man. The clincher: **a hard prostate nodule + a markedly raised prostate-specific antigen (PSA) + sclerotic (osteoblastic) bone lesions**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease; almost all prostate cancers are adenocarcinomas.

nodes.q: Which layer of cells, present in benign prostate glands, is missing from his cancerous glands?
nodes.note: Benign glands have two layers (basal cells under secretory cells); cancer glands have only one. Perineural invasion is another classic finding.

nodes.q: In which zone of the prostate does it usually arise, making it palpable through the rectum?
nodes.a: Peripheral zone (posterior part of the gland)
nodes.note: Benign prostatic hyperplasia grows in the transition zone around the urethra, which is why it causes outlet symptoms earlier.

nodes.q: Which serum marker is raised?
nodes.note: A serine protease made by prostate epithelium that liquefies semen. It is not specific: benign prostatic hyperplasia and prostatitis raise it too. A positive PSA stain on a metastasis proves a prostate origin, as in his lymph node.

nodes.q: Which organ is the most characteristic site of metastasis?
nodes.note: Sclerotic (osteoblastic) lesions in the spine, pelvis, ribs and proximal femur, with a raised alkaline phosphatase.

nodes.q: Which venous route carries tumor cells directly to the vertebrae?
nodes.note: A valveless network that connects with the prostatic venous plexus, so flow reverses with a cough or strain.

nodes.q: His rib broke after only a cough. What kind of fracture is this?
nodes.note: A break through bone already weakened by tumor, from a force that would not break normal bone.

nodes.q: Which emergency follows when a vertebral metastasis collapses backward?
nodes.note: Worsening back pain, then leg weakness, a sensory level and urinary retention. Untreated, it leaves permanent paralysis.

nodes.q: Which drug is given at once while urgent spine imaging is arranged?
nodes.note: Then magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the whole spine, followed by radiation or surgical decompression.

nodes.q: Which features of the tumor set its grade?
nodes.a: Gland architecture and cell appearance (Gleason score)
nodes.note: The Gleason score adds the two most common glandular patterns. Capsule penetration, lymph node involvement, metastasis and size belong to the stage, not the grade.

nodes.q: His node shows uniform, well-formed glands with small, bland nuclei. How is his tumor classified by grade and by stage?
nodes.note: Well-formed glands with bland nuclei are well differentiated (low grade); a lymph node metastasis is advanced (high) stage. Grade and stage are separate.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Core needle biopsy of the prostate, guided by transrectal ultrasound
nodes.note: It follows a hard nodule or a raised or rising PSA. Screening PSA in men aged 55 to 69 is a shared decision.

nodes.q: Which treatments aim to cure disease confined to the prostate?
nodes.note: Low-risk disease in an older man can be watched (active surveillance). Disease that has spread to bone, as in this man, is treated with hormone therapy.

nodes.q: During radical prostatectomy, which structures are at greatest risk of injury?

nodes.note: They run along the back and sides of the prostate and drive erection, so injury causes erectile dysfunction. The obturator nerves lie on the pelvic wall and are at risk in nodal dissection, not in removing the prostate.

nodes.q: Which drug class, given as a monthly depot injection, lowers testosterone because it acts continuously rather than in pulses?

nodes.note: Testosterone and dihydrotestosterone (DHT) can bind the receptor but cannot act.

root.stem: A 62-year-old woman has had 4 months of vaginal bleeding; her periods stopped at age 55. nodes.q: Which test gives the tissue diagnosis of a breast lump?

nodes.q: Which test is used to screen women at average risk?

nodes.q: Which monoclonal antibody targets her HER2-positive tumor?

root.stem: A 27-year-old woman has had 9 months of increasing facial hair, acne, a deeper voice and no menstrual periods. Her clitoris is enlarged. Computed tomography (CT) of the pelvis shows a solid 6-cm mass in the left ovary; the right ovary is normal. Serum testosterone is 450 ng/dL (normal 20 to 60), dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate is normal, and luteinizing hormone is low. Her hemoglobin is 16.4 g/dL. She has no breast enlargement and no bleeding between periods.
root.oneliner: 27F + 9 months of facial hair, acne, deeper voice + absent periods + enlarged clitoris + solid 6-cm left ovarian mass, normal right ovary + testosterone 450 ng/dL + normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate + low luteinizing hormone + hemoglobin 16.4 + no breast enlargement, no intermenstrual bleeding
highlight: solid 6-cm mass in the left ovary

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A rare ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor that makes androgens; it occurs mostly in young women and can virilize girls before puberty. The clincher: **a unilateral solid ovarian mass with virilization (facial hair, deep voice, clitoral enlargement) and a very high testosterone with a normal adrenal androgen**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All the names mean the same tumor, named for its masculinizing effect.

nodes.q: From which ovarian cell line does it arise?
nodes.note: Not from the germ cells and not from the surface epithelium.

nodes.q: Which cells in the tumor make her testosterone?
nodes.note: Steroid-producing cells with pink cytoplasm, sometimes holding Reinke crystals; the Sertoli cells form tubules. Her normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate points to the ovary, not the adrenal gland, as the source.

nodes.q: Why are her periods absent?
nodes.a: Androgen excess suppresses the pituitary release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), so ovulation stops
nodes.note: This explains the low luteinizing hormone. Excess androgen also opposes estrogen action on the endometrium.

nodes.q: Which of her blood values is raised by the testosterone?
nodes.note: Testosterone stimulates erythropoietin release and red cell production. It lowers high-density lipoprotein cholesterol and follicle-stimulating hormone; it does not raise alkaline phosphatase, and prostate-specific antigen needs a prostate.

nodes.q: Which gene mutation is linked with a hereditary form of this tumor in young women?
nodes.note: Part of the DICER1 syndrome, which also brings thyroid and pleuropulmonary tumors.

nodes.q: What is the treatment in a young woman who still wants children?
nodes.note: Stage 1 tumors are usually low grade and cured by surgery; chemotherapy is reserved for advanced or high-grade disease. Testosterone falls after surgery and hair growth slows, but a deep voice may stay.

nodes.q: Her ovarian mass could be a granulosa cell tumor. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Excess estrogen**: precocious puberty in girls, breast enlargement, endometrial hyperplasia and bleeding; Call-Exner bodies, raised inhibin
**Excess androgens**: facial hair, deep voice, clitoral enlargement, absent periods; no breast enlargement or bleeding

nodes.note: The trap: both are ovarian sex cord-stromal tumors, but one feminizes and the other masculinizes.

nodes.q: Her facial hair and absent periods could suggest polycystic ovary syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Irregular periods since menarche + obesity + bilateral small cysts**; only a mild rise in testosterone, high luteinizing hormone to follicle-stimulating hormone ratio
**Rapid onset within months + unilateral solid mass + testosterone above 200 ng/dL with low luteinizing hormone**

nodes.q: Her androgen excess could come from the adrenal gland. How do you tell the source apart?

split.a: Adrenal androgen source (adrenal tumor or congenital adrenal hyperplasia)
split.note: **High dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate**; adrenal mass on imaging; normal ovaries
**Normal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate with very high testosterone + ovarian mass**

root.stem: A 52-year-old man has had 3 days of fever to 39.2°C, chills, burning on urination and deep pelvic pain. He now urinates every hour, dribbles, and feels his bladder never empties. He has had no urethral discharge, no testicular pain or swelling, no blood in the urine and no trauma. He is sexually active only with his wife. The penis and scrotum look normal. On rectal examination the prostate is enlarged, exquisitely tender and boggy. Urine culture grows gram-negative rods that ferment lactose.
root.oneliner: 52M + 3 days of fever 39.2°C, chills + dysuria + deep pelvic pain + hourly urination, dribbling, incomplete emptying + no urethral discharge, no testicular pain, no hematuria, no trauma + monogamous + normal penis and scrotum + enlarged, exquisitely tender, boggy prostate + urine culture: lactose-fermenting gram-negative rods
highlight: sexually active only with his wife

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Infection of the prostate gland. The clincher: **fever and chills + urinary symptoms + an exquisitely tender, boggy prostate on rectal examination**.

nodes.q: Which organism most likely causes it at his age?
nodes.note: A lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod that makes pink colonies on MacConkey agar. After catheterization or prostate procedures, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and other gram-negative rods become more likely.

nodes.q: How do the bacteria usually reach the prostate?
nodes.a: Reflux of infected urine from the urethra into the prostatic ducts
nodes.note: Intraprostatic reflux; less often spread from the rectum or blood.

nodes.q: Why does he dribble and feel his bladder never empties?
nodes.a: The swollen prostate compresses the urethra and obstructs urine outflow
nodes.note: Complete blockage causes acute urinary retention. (Step 2: drain with a suprapubic catheter rather than pass a urethral one through the inflamed gland.)

nodes.q: Which part of the rectal examination should be avoided?
nodes.note: It can push bacteria into the blood and cause sepsis. Send a urine culture instead.

nodes.q: Which antibiotic class is the usual first choice because it reaches the inflamed prostate well and covers his organism?
nodes.note: Give for 2 to 4 weeks; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the alternative. Admit and give intravenous antibiotics if he is septic.

nodes.q: Which bacterial enzymes do fluoroquinolones inhibit?
nodes.a: DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV
nodes.note: Bactericidal. Adverse effects: tendon rupture (Achilles), QT prolongation, cartilage damage in children; avoid with antacids containing calcium, magnesium or aluminum.

nodes.q: Which complication is suspected when fever continues despite 48 to 72 hours of the right antibiotic?
nodes.note: Confirm with transrectal ultrasound or CT of the pelvis and drain it.

nodes.q: Chlamydia infection can also cause pelvic pain and urinary symptoms. How do you tell it apart?

split.note: Age **under 35 + new sexual partners + urethral discharge**; epididymitis; treat with doxycycline; Ureaplasma urealyticum behaves the same way
Age **over 35 + obstructive urinary symptoms + tender boggy prostate**; no urethral discharge

nodes.note: The trap: both cause urinary frequency and dysuria, but sexually transmitted organisms cause prostatitis mainly in younger men.

nodes.q: Gonorrhea could also cause dysuria. How do you tell it apart?

split.note: **Purulent urethral discharge** within days of a new partner; gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils
**No discharge; fever + tender boggy prostate**; lactose-fermenting rods

nodes.q: His dribbling and frequency could suggest benign prostatic hyperplasia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Months to years of slow stream; afebrile; smooth, firm, nontender, rubbery prostate**
**Days of fever + exquisitely tender, boggy prostate**

nodes.q: Mumps can inflame the male genital tract. How do you tell it apart?

split.note: **Painful swollen testis**, usually with parotid swelling days earlier; prostate not tender
**Normal testes and scrotum; tender prostate; urinary symptoms**

root.stem: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 2, has had 4 days of pain in the right vulva that makes walking and sitting hard. Her last menstrual period was 1 week ago. She has had no trauma, no previous vaginal infections and no urinary symptoms. She is afebrile. Examination shows an acutely tender, fluctuant 3-cm mass at the posterior vaginal opening that distends the right labium majus and seems to point toward the vagina. The mass lies away from the urethral opening, the skin of the vulva is otherwise normal, and there is no ulcer.
root.oneliner: 26F G2P2 + 4 days of right vulvar pain + no trauma, no prior vaginal infections, no urinary symptoms + afebrile + tender fluctuant 3-cm mass at posterior vaginal opening distending right labium majus, pointing toward vagina + away from urethral opening + normal vulvar skin, no ulcer

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An infected, blocked Bartholin gland duct. The clincher: **a tender, fluctuant mass at the posterior vaginal opening (4 or 8 o'clock) that distends the labium majus**.

nodes.q: What do the Bartholin glands (greater vestibular glands) secrete?
nodes.a: Mucus that lubricates the vaginal opening
nodes.note: They sit on each side of the vaginal opening and drain by a duct at the 4 and 8 o'clock positions.

nodes.q: Which male gland is the homologue of the Bartholin gland?
nodes.note: Both are mucus-secreting glands that arise from the urogenital sinus.

nodes.q: What event starts the process?
nodes.note: Mucus builds up into a cyst, which becomes infected.

nodes.q: Which organisms usually cause the infection?
nodes.a: Mixed (polymicrobial) vaginal and bowel flora, including Escherichia coli
nodes.note: Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis are less common causes; test for them in a sexually active woman.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Incision and drainage with placement of a Word catheter
nodes.note: The balloon catheter stays 4 to 6 weeks so a new duct opening forms. Antibiotics only if cellulitis, immunosuppression or a sexually transmitted infection; marsupialization for repeated abscesses.

nodes.q: Which tumor must be excluded in a woman over 40 with a new Bartholin mass?
nodes.note: Biopsy any solid or persistent mass in this age group.

nodes.q: Her mass could be a Skene gland cyst. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Beside the urethral opening**, anterior; may cause urinary obstruction or dysuria
**Posterior at 4 or 8 o'clock, distending the labium majus**; away from the urethra

nodes.note: The trap: both are glandular duct blockages of the vestibule.

nodes.q: Her mass could be an epidermal inclusion cyst. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small, painless, firm, in the skin of the labium**; follows trauma or episiotomy; no fluctuance toward the vagina
**Acutely tender, fluctuant, posterior vaginal opening mass**

nodes.q: Her lump could be vulvar carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Older woman, persistent ulcer or plaque, itching, human papillomavirus or lichen sclerosus**; firm, not fluctuant
**Reproductive age, 4 days of pain, tender fluctuant mass, normal skin without an ulcer**

nodes.q: Her lump could be a vulvar hematoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden after trauma or childbirth**; blue-black, expanding, tense
**No trauma + gradual onset over days + fluctuant mass**

root.stem: A 28-year-old woman has had 4 months of mild left lower abdominal fullness. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 7-cm cystic left ovarian mass with a bright echogenic nodule that casts a shadow behind it. The mass is removed. It contains a greasy yellow material and tufts of hair. Under the microscope there are cysts lined by stratified squamous epithelium, mature cartilage and mature glands. There is no immature neural tissue and no sign of invasion. Her serum alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin are normal.
root.oneliner: 28F + 4 months of left lower abdominal fullness + 7-cm cystic ovarian mass with bright echogenic nodule and acoustic shadowing + greasy yellow material and hair + cysts lined by stratified squamous epithelium, mature cartilage and mature glands + no immature neural tissue, no invasion + normal alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin
highlight: bright echogenic nodule that casts a shadow
greasy yellow material and tufts of hair
alpha-fetoprotein and human chorionic gonadotropin are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Mature cystic teratoma of the ovary
nodes.note: The commonest ovarian germ cell tumor and a benign one. The clincher: **a cystic ovarian mass with mature tissues from more than one germ layer (skin with hair, cartilage, glands)**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The skin-lined cyst full of hair and sebum gives the name.

nodes.q: From how many germ layers does the tissue in the mass derive?
nodes.a: All three: ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm
nodes.note: Her squamous epithelium is ectoderm, the cartilage is mesoderm and the glands are endoderm.

nodes.q: Which karyotype do the tumor cells usually have?
nodes.note: The tumor arises from a single germ cell (oocyte line) that has completed the first meiotic division; it is not a fertilized embryo.

nodes.q: What is the name of the shadowing echogenic nodule on her ultrasound?
nodes.note: A plug of hair, fat, bone or teeth projecting into the cyst. A fat-fluid level or lines of hair may also show.

nodes.q: Which complication causes sudden severe one-sided pelvic pain with vomiting?
nodes.note: The heavy mass twists on its pedicle and cuts off the blood supply; this is the commonest complication, and untreated it leads to infarction and loss of the ovary. Treat with emergency laparoscopic detorsion.

nodes.q: What is the usual treatment?
nodes.a: Ovarian cystectomy that spares the ovary
nodes.note: Done laparoscopically in a young woman; spill of the greasy contents can cause a chemical peritonitis.

nodes.q: Which cancer rarely develops inside the mass in an older woman?
nodes.note: From the squamous lining, in about 1 to 2 percent of cases.

nodes.q: Which tissue, if it dominates, can cause hyperthyroidism?
nodes.note: A teratoma made mostly of functioning thyroid tissue.

nodes.q: Which autoimmune brain disease is associated with this tumor in young women?
nodes.note: Antibodies against the NMDA receptor on neural tissue in the tumor; presents with psychosis, seizures, abnormal movements and autonomic instability. Removing the tumor helps.

nodes.q: The cartilage in the mass could suggest a chondrosarcoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Only cartilage, malignant**, usually in the pelvis or long bones of older people; no hair, skin or glands
**Cartilage together with skin, hair and glands in one cystic mass**

nodes.note: The trap: a single tissue type cannot explain hair and glands. A chondroma is the benign single-tissue version.

nodes.q: The glands in the mass could suggest an adenocarcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Glands only, with atypia and invasion**; solid areas; raised tumor markers
**Mature glands mixed with squamous cysts and cartilage; no invasion**

nodes.q: A young woman's ovarian teratoma could be immature. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Adolescent or young girl + large solid mass + immature neuroepithelial tissue**; raised alpha-fetoprotein; malignant
**Cystic mass + only mature tissues + normal tumor markers**; benign

root.stem: A newborn boy is the larger of identical twin boys delivered at 34 weeks to a 27-year-old woman. He is ruddy and plethoric with a hematocrit of 68%, and he weighs 2,300 g. His smaller co-twin is pale and lethargic with a hematocrit of 28%, and weighs 1,700 g. The twins shared one placenta and had separate amniotic sacs. An ultrasound at 20 weeks showed too much amniotic fluid around one twin and too little around the other. There was no maternal bleeding, the umbilical cords are not knotted, and the cords and membranes show no inflammation.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy, larger of identical twins delivered at 34 weeks + ruddy, plethoric, hematocrit 68% + co-twin pale, lethargic, hematocrit 28%, smaller + one placenta, separate amniotic sacs + ultrasound at 20 weeks: too much fluid around one twin, too little around the other + no maternal bleeding, no cord knots, no inflammation
highlight: ruddy and plethoric with a hematocrit of 68%
pale and lethargic with a hematocrit of 28%
too much amniotic fluid around one twin and too little around the other

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Unequal blood flow between identical twins that share a placenta. The clincher: **monochorionic twins with a plethoric recipient and a pale donor, plus too much fluid around one and too little around the other**.

nodes.q: Which kind of placental vessel connection carries blood one way from the donor twin to the recipient twin?
nodes.note: An artery from the donor supplies a cotyledon deep in the shared placenta that drains into a vein of the recipient, so flow goes only one way. Surface artery-to-artery anastomoses carry blood both ways and protect against the syndrome; few or none of them raises the risk. Exam options may simply say 'placental (chorionic) vascular anastomoses' or even 'artery-to-artery anastomoses' (REPROD-0125): pick the option naming vascular connections between the twins, because none of the others (membrane fluid leak, abruption, funisitis, knotted cords, oligohydramnios) can move blood from one twin to the other.

nodes.q: Which type of placenta allows these connections?
nodes.note: Dichorionic twins have separate placentas, so the syndrome cannot occur.

nodes.q: On which days after fertilization does the zygote split in a monochorionic diamniotic pregnancy?
nodes.note: Before day 4 gives two chorions and two amnions; after day 8 gives one chorion and one amnion; after day 13 gives conjoined twins.

nodes.q: Which fluid abnormality surrounds the recipient twin?
nodes.note: Volume overload makes the recipient pass large amounts of urine. The donor, with less volume, makes little urine and has oligohydramnios (a stuck twin).

nodes.q: Which problem does a hematocrit of 68% cause in the larger twin's blood?
nodes.note: Thick, slow-flowing blood risks thrombosis, poor feeding, hypoglycemia and jaundice from red cell breakdown. (Step 2: symptomatic polycythemia is treated with partial exchange transfusion.)

nodes.q: What does the volume overload do to the recipient twin's heart before birth?
nodes.a: Heart failure, which can progress to hydrops fetalis
nodes.note: The recipient is the twin more likely to die in utero; ventricular hypertrophy and tricuspid regurgitation are seen on fetal echocardiography.

nodes.q: Why is the smaller twin pale?
nodes.a: Anemia from chronic blood loss to the co-twin
nodes.note: The donor also has growth restriction and, in the womb, kidney injury from low perfusion. (Step 2: treat with a red cell transfusion.)

nodes.q: How are monochorionic twins followed in pregnancy?
nodes.a: Ultrasound every 2 weeks starting at 16 weeks
nodes.note: Look for discordant fluid in the two sacs; stage with Quintero staging.

nodes.q: Which fetal treatment is used for severe disease before 26 weeks?
nodes.a: Fetoscopic laser ablation of the connecting vessels
nodes.note: It separates the two circulations; amnioreduction is a second option.

nodes.q: Their different hematocrits could suggest twin anemia polycythemia sequence. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Large hemoglobin difference with normal amniotic fluid in both sacs**; slow flow through tiny connections, often after laser or in late pregnancy
**Hemoglobin difference plus polyhydramnios and oligohydramnios**

nodes.note: The trap: both are monochorionic transfusion problems.

nodes.q: The smaller twin's growth and low fluid could suggest chronic placental abruption. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Maternal bleeding or retroplacental clot**; oligohydramnios and growth restriction; no polycythemic twin
**No bleeding; one plethoric twin and one pale twin**

nodes.q: One pale twin could result from knotted umbilical cords. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden loss of blood flow with fetal distress or stillbirth**; no hematocrit difference or fluid difference
**Discordant hematocrits and amniotic fluid with intact cords**

nodes.q: Inflammation of the cords could also affect the twins. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Maternal fever, foul-smelling fluid, neutrophils in the cord**; both twins affected by infection
**No infection; blood volume shifted from donor to recipient**

root.stem: A 58-year-old woman found a lump in her left breast two days ago. She went through menopause 6 years back, has four children, has never been a smoker, and reports no trauma to or operation on the breast. For some time the left nipple has leaked a thick, tacky, green-tinged fluid from multiple duct openings, and it has become retracted. A 1-cm irregular, firm nodule lies in the tissue around the left areola; she has no fever and the skin is not red. On mammography there is a hazy density worrisome for cancer, and core needle sampling is not diagnostic. Pathology of the resected lesion shows a markedly enlarged duct with a glandular lining, encircled by dense infiltrating lymphocytes and plasma cells, its lumen packed with foamy lipid-filled macrophages and amorphous debris.
root.oneliner: 58F + new left breast lump + menopause 6 years ago + four children, never smoked, no breast injury or surgery + thick sticky greenish discharge from several ducts + nipple turned inward + 1-cm poorly circumscribed periareolar mass + no fever, no redness + ill-defined density on mammography, nondiagnostic needle biopsy + excised: dilated duct, lymphocytes and plasma cells, lumen with lipid-laden macrophages and debris
highlight: no trauma to or operation on the breast
thick, tacky, green-tinged fluid from multiple duct openings
1-cm irregular, firm nodule lies in the tissue around the left areola
no fever and the skin is not red
core needle sampling is not diagnostic
markedly enlarged duct with a glandular lining
dense infiltrating lymphocytes and plasma cells
foamy lipid-filled macrophages and amorphous debris

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Dilation of the large ducts beneath the nipple with inflammation around them. The clincher: **a periareolar mass in a menopausal woman with a dilated duct full of lipid-laden macrophages and debris, ringed by plasma cells**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names mean the same disease; the plasma cells give the second name.

nodes.q: What fills the dilated duct on microscopy?
nodes.note: Secretions stagnate and leak into the surrounding tissue, which draws in plasma cells and lymphocytes and later causes fibrosis.

nodes.q: In which group of women does it typically occur?
nodes.a: Older, multiparous women around or after menopause (fifth and sixth decades)
nodes.note: Unlike periductal mastitis, it is not linked with smoking.

nodes.q: Which nipple change from scarring can mimic cancer?
nodes.note: The fibrosis around the ducts pulls the nipple inward. Together with a mass and an ill-defined density it can look like cancer, which is why tissue is needed.

nodes.q: What is the next step when a needle biopsy of a suspicious mass is nondiagnostic?
nodes.note: The mass is removed whole to exclude cancer, as was done here. The disease itself is benign and does not raise cancer risk.

nodes.q: Her mass and nipple change could suggest intraductal carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Clustered fine calcifications; atypical cells filling the duct; bloody discharge from one duct**; no plasma cell inflammation
**Thick greenish discharge from several ducts + dilated duct with foamy macrophages + plasma cells**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a periareolar finding that looks suspicious on mammography.

nodes.q: Her lump could be a fibroadenoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Young woman; mobile, rubbery, well-circumscribed lump**; stroma and glands on biopsy
**Menopausal woman; poorly circumscribed periareolar mass; nipple retraction**

nodes.q: Her breast lump could be fibrocystic change. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Premenopausal; both breasts lumpy and tender with the cycle**; cysts, fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia
**Menopausal; one subareolar mass; discharge from several ducts**

nodes.q: Her breast could be acutely infected. How do you tell acute mastitis apart?

split.note: **Breastfeeding woman; fever, a red, hot, tender breast**; Staphylococcus aureus
**Menopausal; no fever and no redness**; thick discharge and chronic plasma cell infiltrate

nodes.q: Nipple discharge could come from an intraductal papilloma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Bloody discharge from a single duct**; small mass near the nipple in a woman of 35 to 55
**Thick greenish discharge from several ducts**; nipple retraction

nodes.q: Her subareolar inflammation could suggest periductal mastitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Smoker + keratinizing squamous metaplasia of the lactiferous ducts with keratin plugs**; recurrent subareolar abscess and fistula to the areola
**Nonsmoking menopausal woman + dilated duct with lipid-laden macrophages and plasma cells**; no squamous metaplasia

nodes.note: Both sit under the nipple and can retract it; smoking and squamous metaplasia belong to periductal mastitis.

nodes.q: Her ill-defined mass full of foamy macrophages could suggest fat necrosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Previous trauma, surgery or radiation + necrotic fat cells with saponification and calcium**; macrophages lie in the fat, not in a duct
**No injury; macrophages and debris fill a dilated duct ringed by plasma cells**

root.stem: A 26-year-old man noticed a painless, firm 2-cm nodule in his right testis 3 months ago. It is hard to separate from the testis, does not light up when a penlight is held behind the scrotum, and is not tender. He has no fever, urinary symptoms or groin swelling. His right testis was brought down into the scrotum by surgery at age 3. Ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass. Serum alpha-fetoprotein is normal, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin is mildly raised and lactate dehydrogenase is raised. The surgical specimen shows sheets of uniform large cells with clear cytoplasm separated by thin fibrous bands full of lymphocytes.
root.oneliner: 26M + painless firm 2-cm testicular nodule, hard to separate from the testis, does not transilluminate + undescended testis fixed at age 3 + solid intratesticular mass on ultrasound + normal alpha-fetoprotein, mildly raised beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, raised lactate dehydrogenase + sheets of uniform clear cells with lymphocytes
highlight: hard to separate from the testis
brought down into the scrotum by surgery at age 3
sheets of uniform large cells with clear cytoplasm

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A cancer of the cells that make sperm and the most common cancer in young men. The clincher: **a painless, firm nodule that is part of the testis and does not transilluminate**.

nodes.q: Which examination finding shows the nodule is solid and not a fluid-filled sac?
nodes.note: Fluid-filled sacs such as a hydrocele or a cyst light up; a solid mass blocks the light. A painless solid testicular mass is cancer until proven otherwise.

nodes.q: Which developmental problem of his testis is the strongest risk factor?
nodes.note: The risk stays raised after surgical fixation and also affects the normally descended testis on the other side. Klinefelter syndrome, a previous germ cell tumor and a family history add risk. Mumps orchitis, varicocele, vasectomy and alcohol are not risk factors.

nodes.q: Which subtype fits his sheets of uniform clear cells with lymphocytes and a normal alpha-fetoprotein?
nodes.note: The most common germ cell tumor, with a peak in the 30s. The cells look like fried eggs and carry placental alkaline phosphatase and OCT4. A few syncytiotrophoblast-like cells explain the mild rise in beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG). Seminoma never makes alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).

nodes.q: A very high alpha-fetoprotein would point to which germ cell component instead?
nodes.note: Look for Schiller-Duval bodies (a central vessel inside a space lined by tumor cells). Seminoma does not make this protein.

nodes.q: What is the group of all the other germ cell tumors called?
nodes.a: Nonseminomatous germ cell tumors (embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma, teratoma)
nodes.note: They appear earlier (20s), grow faster, often mix several cell types and are much less sensitive to radiation. Embryonal carcinoma is hemorrhagic with pleomorphic cells in glands and sheets. Teratoma in an adult man is malignant, unlike the benign mature teratoma of the ovary.

nodes.q: Which of them spreads early through the blood to the lungs and makes a very high beta-human chorionic gonadotropin?
nodes.note: Hemorrhagic, made of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast. The hormone can cause gynecomastia and, because it resembles thyroid-stimulating hormone, hyperthyroidism.

nodes.q: Which lymph node group receives metastases from the testis first?
nodes.note: The testis forms high in the abdomen near the kidney and keeps its lymph drainage and blood supply from there. Scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes instead, which is why the scrotum is never cut or biopsied.

nodes.q: What is the first operation?
nodes.note: Done through the groin with high tying off of the cord, not through the scrotum. Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen and pelvis stages the disease, tumor markers are repeated after surgery, and sperm banking is offered beforehand.

nodes.q: The testis and cord wear coverings borrowed from the abdominal wall. Which abdominal layer gives the outermost fascial covering, the external spermatic fascia?
nodes.note: The internal oblique gives the cremasteric muscle and fascia, the transversalis fascia gives the internal spermatic fascia, and the peritoneum gives the tunica vaginalis. The dartos muscle lies in the scrotal skin layer.

nodes.q: To which treatment is seminoma especially sensitive?
nodes.note: Seminoma is very radiosensitive and very chemosensitive, with cure rates above 90% even with spread. After orchiectomy, early disease is watched or given radiation or single-dose carboplatin. Nonseminomatous tumors are treated with cisplatin-based chemotherapy and sometimes retroperitoneal lymph node dissection.

nodes.q: Which combination chemotherapy is used for spread or nonseminomatous disease?
nodes.note: Bleomycin causes pulmonary fibrosis, cisplatin causes kidney damage, nerve damage and hearing loss, and etoposide blocks topoisomerase II.

nodes.q: Some regimens replace bleomycin with ifosfamide. Which bladder toxicity does ifosfamide cause?
nodes.note: The liver turns ifosfamide into a metabolite, acrolein, which injures the bladder lining. Cyclophosphamide does the same.

nodes.q: Which drug is given with ifosfamide to prevent it?
nodes.note: A thiol that binds acrolein in the urine. It does not protect against the drug's other toxicities such as bone marrow suppression.

nodes.q: His painless scrotal swelling could suggest a hydrocele. How do you tell them apart?

**Firm nodule that is part of the testis and does not transilluminate**; ultrasound shows a solid intratesticular mass

nodes.note: The trap: both are painless scrotal swellings.

nodes.q: A scrotal lump could be a varicocele. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **'Bag of worms' above the testis, usually on the left, bigger standing and shrinking when lying down**
**Fixed firm nodule in the testis that does not change with position**

nodes.q: A scrotal mass could be testicular torsion. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden severe pain, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex**, usually in an adolescent
**Painless firm nodule over weeks to months** with a normal cremasteric reflex

nodes.q: A testicular mass could be a Leydig cell tumor. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Golden-brown mass with Reinke crystals** that makes androgens or estrogens: gynecomastia in adults, early puberty in boys
**Sheets of uniform clear cells with lymphocytes**; no hormone-driven body changes

nodes.q: A scrotal swelling could be epididymitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painful, swollen epididymis with fever and pyuria**; pain eases when the testis is lifted
**Painless, no fever, no urinary symptoms**; the mass is in the testis itself

nodes.q: A scrotal lump could be a spermatocele or scrotal cyst. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Smooth cystic lump above and separate from the testis that transilluminates**
**Solid nodule that cannot be separated from the testis and does not transilluminate**

nodes.q: His history could tempt you to name an undescended testis as the diagnosis. How do you tell them apart?

root.stem: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus has had 3 weeks of vulvar itching, burning during intercourse and a thick white discharge. She finished a course of antibiotics for a urinary tract infection 2 weeks ago. She has had one partner for 25 years and he has no symptoms. Examination shows red, swollen vaginal mucosa with a thick white curd-like discharge that sticks to the wall. The vaginal pH is 4.2 and no fishy odor appears when potassium hydroxide is added. A potassium hydroxide wet mount shows budding yeast and branching filaments.

highlight: antibiotics for a urinary tract infection

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A yeast infection of the vagina and vulva. The clincher: **itching with a thick, white, curd-like discharge, a normal vaginal pH (4.0 to 4.5) and budding yeast with pseudohyphae on microscopy**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All three names describe the same infection.

nodes.q: Which organism most often causes it?
nodes.note: A normal commensal of the mouth, gut and vagina that forms germ tubes at 37 °C. Species such as Candida glabrata are often resistant to azole drugs.

nodes.q: Which chronic disease in her history predisposes her to it?
nodes.note: High glucose in tissues and secretions feeds the yeast. Pregnancy, estrogen therapy and immunosuppression also raise the risk.

nodes.q: How did her recent antibiotics lead to the infection?
nodes.a: They killed protective vaginal lactobacilli, letting yeast overgrow
nodes.note: Lactobacilli make lactic acid that keeps competitors in check. Yeast tolerate the acid, so the pH stays normal, unlike in bacterial vaginosis.

nodes.q: Which bedside test confirms it?
nodes.a: Potassium hydroxide wet mount showing budding yeast and pseudohyphae
nodes.note: The potassium hydroxide dissolves the epithelial cells and leaves the fungal elements visible. Culture is kept for repeated infections.

nodes.q: Which oral drug treats it?
nodes.note: A single dose is enough for uncomplicated disease. Topical azoles such as clotrimazole or miconazole also work and are used in pregnancy, when oral azoles are avoided.

nodes.q: How does fluconazole kill the yeast?
nodes.a: It inhibits the fungal cytochrome P450 enzyme lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase, blocking ergosterol synthesis
nodes.note: Ergosterol is the main sterol of the fungal cell membrane. Other antifungal actions: amphotericin B and nystatin form pores in the membrane, echinocandins block beta-glucan synthesis in the cell wall, flucytosine blocks DNA and RNA synthesis. Azoles also inhibit human cytochrome P450 enzymes, so drug interactions and liver injury occur.

nodes.q: Her itching, redness and discharge could suggest trichomoniasis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Frothy yellow-green discharge, pH above 4.5, motile flagellated protozoa on wet mount**, sometimes a strawberry cervix; sexually transmitted, so the partner is treated
**Thick white curd-like discharge, normal pH, budding yeast with pseudohyphae**; not sexually transmitted

nodes.note: The trap: both cause itching and a red, inflamed vagina.

nodes.q: Her discharge could suggest bacterial vaginosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Thin grey-white discharge, pH above 4.5, fishy odor with potassium hydroxide, clue cells**; little itching or inflammation
**Itching, red swollen mucosa, thick white discharge, normal pH, no fishy odor**

nodes.q: Her vaginal symptoms could come from chlamydial infection. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Mucopurulent cervical discharge and cervicitis, often silent; intracellular inclusions or a positive nucleic acid test**; no yeast
**Thick white curd-like vaginal discharge with budding yeast and pseudohyphae**

nodes.q: Her burning and soreness could suggest genital herpes. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painful grouped vesicles that break into shallow ulcers, with tender nodes**; multinucleated giant cells on a Tzanck smear
**Itching with white discharge and no vesicles or ulcers**

nodes.q: Her vulvar symptoms could come from human papillomavirus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless warty growths (condylomata) or koilocytes on a Pap smear**; no curd-like discharge
**Itching, red mucosa and yeast on microscopy**; no warts
